title: ISO Exam Traps — Every Confusion Pair in One Place
shortDescription: Every 'these two sound the same but aren't' pair from this subject, collected into one dedicated traps sheet.
genZNote: If two ISO things sound like synonyms, they're probably this page's next entry.

table.caption: Read each row as 'don't confuse A with B'
rows: ISO writes standards; it never certifies any company, product, or person itself.
Certification checks an ORGANIZATION against a standard; accreditation checks a CERTIFICATION BODY's own competence to do that.
ISO is the international standards body; BIS is India's national standards body and ISO's India member — BIS adapts, it doesn't replace, ISO.
BIS sets/adapts standards and runs its own product certification (ISI mark); NABL accredits testing/calibration/medical laboratories — different jobs entirely.
9001 is the certifiable requirements standard; 9000 is only the vocabulary/concepts document — not certifiable.
15189 is medical-laboratory-specific (pre/examination/post phases); 17025 is general testing/calibration lab competence (management + technical requirements).
HACCP is a hazard-control METHOD, not an ISO standard; ISO 22000 is a full, certifiable Food Safety Management System that incorporates HACCP as one component.
14001 manages an organization's impact ON the environment (aspect → impact); 45001 manages risks TO its own workers (hazard → risk).
ISO covers almost all fields except electrical/electronic engineering, which is IEC's domain — they co-publish standards like ISO/IEC 17025 and 27001 where scopes overlap.
A management system standard (e.g. ISO 9001) defines HOW an organization runs a system; a product standard defines technical requirements for a specific PRODUCT.
A testing lab (materials, environmental, general) seeks ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation; a medical/clinical lab seeks ISO 15189 accreditation.
31000 (risk) and 19011 (audit guidance) are GUIDANCE documents — you cannot be 'certified' against either one.

sections.heading: If You Only Remember One Rule From This Whole Subject
sections.body: ISO develops standards. Independent certification bodies certify organizations against those standards. Accreditation bodies certify that the certification bodies are themselves competent. Government regulation, where it exists, decides whether following a standard is optional or mandatory. Four separate layers — and almost every ISO exam trap is really just a version of mixing up which layer a fact belongs to.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: This topic is a consolidated list of the confusion pairs across the ISO subject — each one traces back to mixing up standard-setting, certification, and accreditation, or mixing up two similarly-scoped standards.
keyFacts: ISO never certifies anyone — certification bodies do, and accreditation bodies check the certification bodies.
BIS (standards) and NABL (laboratory accreditation) are different roles in India's ecosystem.
9000 (vocabulary) vs 9001 (requirements); 15189 (medical labs) vs 17025 (general labs); 14001 (environment) vs 45001 (worker safety) are the three most common standard-vs-standard trap pairs.
commonConfusion: Every row of the trap table above is, by definition, a common confusion — treat the whole table as this topic's confusion list.

highYieldFacts: The four-layer chain (standard → certification → accreditation → regulation) resolves almost every ISO exam trap when applied directly.
Standard-vs-standard traps (9000/9001, 15189/17025, 14001/45001, ISO 22000/HACCP) are the second most common trap category after the certification/accreditation confusion.
commonTraps: Treat every row in the trap table as independently testable — exams often ask these as direct 'A vs B, what's the difference' questions.
Don't assume a trap pair is 'basically the same thing' just because the names sound similar — that similarity is exactly what the question is testing.
mustRemember: When stuck between two similar-sounding ISO facts, ask: which LAYER (standard/certification/accreditation/regulation) does each belong to, and which SCOPE (medical vs general, environment vs safety) does each cover?
possibleQuestions: Explain the difference between certification and accreditation with an example.
A hospital pathology lab and a materials-testing lab each want lab accreditation — which ISO standard does each pursue?
